    <item>

      <link>https://www.nrk.no/nyheter/israel-med-ny-offensiv-_-tre-drept-1.18084431</link>
      <description>Israels hær sier den har innledet en operasjon i Hamas-kontrollerte områder i Gaza
Israel har innledet en militæroperasjon i det sentrale Gaza vest for den såkalte gule linjen, som har skilt Hamas-kontrollerte og israelsk-kontrollerte områder siden våpenhvilen trådte i kraft i fjor. Det opplyser militæret til AFP.
Vitner sier at israelske stridsvogner rullet inn på hovedveien Salahudeen, vest for den såkalte gule linjen som markerer grensen for de to tredjedelene av Gazastripen som fortsatt er under israelsk kontroll.
Den såkalte gule linjen ble etablert etter våpenhvilen i oktober 2025 og skiller israelskkontrollerte og palestinske soner i Gazastripen. Israelske styrker har gradvis flyttet den gule linjen og utvidet området under direkte militær kontroll i Gaza.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Braathen med ny maktdemonstrasjon: – Jeg er så full av følelser</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/sport/braathen-med-ny-maktdemonstrasjon_-_-jeg-er-sa-full-av-folelser-1.18082207</link>
      <description>Norsk-brasilianske Lucas Pinheiro Braathen (26) fortsetter å ydmyke konkurrentene.
Etter seier i storslalåm-starten i Sölden, fortsatte han med seier i slalåm i finske Levi søndag.
– Det er så godt å være her i Levi. Jeg er så full av følelser nå. Jeg skal prøve å ta selvtilliten med meg videre til neste renn, sier Braathen selv i arenaintervjuet.
Clément Noël ble nummer to, 56 hundredeler bak vinneren. Atle Lie McGrath ble beste norske på 7. plass.
– Det er hans bakke. Han elsker den. Han elsker disse forholdene, sier TV 2-ekspert Kjetil Jansrud på direkten.
– Han er fremdeles norsk, men han representerer Brasil. Vi skulle gjerne ha sett det norske flagget bak navnet hans, fortsetter Jansrud.
Dette er den tredje vinteren der Braathen representerer Brasil etter at han brøt med Norges Skiforbund.
– For en kjøring. Det er store, store avstander i en bakke som Levi, sa TV 2-ekspert Jansrud etter Braathens første omgang.
Han ledet med hele 65 hundredeler til toeren, Clément Noël, før finaleomgangen.

– Det Lucas gjør det er helt i egen klasse, sa Timon Haugan til TV 2 etter første omgang.
– Jeg fikk meg en på tygga, sier McGrath om finaleomgangen.
Oscar Andreas Sandvik kjørte seg opp fra 29. plass til nummer 11.
Både Timon Haugan og Henrik Kristoffersen tapte halvannet sekund til Braathen i første omgang. Begge fortsatte å skuffe i andre omgang og ble henholdsvis 18 og 19.
– Jeg kjørte i en stein, forteller Kristoffersen til TV 2.</description>

    <item>
      <title>Vind og kaos-skyting: Kirkeeide vant fellesstarten etter åtte (!) bom</title>
      <link>https://www.nrk.no/sport/vind-og-kaos-skyting_-kirkeeide-vant-fellesstarten-etter-atte-___-bom-1.18082184</link>
      <description>Maren Kirkeeide stakk av med seieren på kvinnenes fellesstart i skiskyting på Geilo søndag.
Lørdagens sprintsensasjon Guro Ytterhus imponerte igjen og tok andreplass 14,4 sekunder bak Kirkeeide.
Juni Arnekleiv ledet etter to fulle hus, men på tredje skyting ble det kaos. Sterk vind gjorde at flere av utøverne bommet mange ganger, og Arnekleiv røk på fire bom.
Dermed tok Karoline Knotten over teten. Men på siste skyting, så haglet skuddene utenfor blinkene nok en gang.
Og plutselig var Kirkeeide i tet etter hele åtte (!) bom. Få løpere måtte ut i flere strafferunder, men likevel holdt hun ledelsen helt til mål.
– Det var en merkelig fellesstart. Det var veldig mange som bommet. Det var tydeligvis ikke så lett som man skulle tro, sier Kirkeeide til NRK etter seieren.
Karoline Knotten tok tredjeplass.
Ingrid Landmark Tandrevold, Marthe Kråkstad Johansen, Karoline Knotten og nevnte Kirkeeide er forhåndsuttatt til verdenscupstarten i finske Kontiolahti senere i måneden. Kvinnenes tropp skal til slutt bestå av seks løpere.</description>

      <description>USAs transportminister Sean Duffy sier utskiftning av en kobbertråd kan være årsaken til den omfattende flystansen fredag.
Flere enn 15.000 flygninger ble forsinket eller innstilt da amerikanske luftfartsmyndigheter FAA i fire timer nektet alle fly å ta av på grunn av forstyrrelser i flykontrollen.
På en pressekonferanse lørdag sa transportminister Duffy at problemene kan ha oppstått som følge av arbeidet med å bytte ut gamle kobberkabler med fiber ved et av FAAs anlegg.
Ministeren oppgav også navnet på selskapet han mente hadde forsårsaket problemene. Hendelsen skal granskes videre.

      <description>Det brenner kraftig i en enebolig på en gård i Trondheimsveien i Lillestrøm.
– Det er full fyr i hele bygningen, opplyser oppdragsleder i politiet, Ronny Mangseth.
– Brannvesenet er fremme og er i gang med slukking. Det er kontroll på alle fire beboere på stedet, sier han.

En person skal ha fått i seg noe røyk.
Det skal ikke være fare for spredning til låve eller andre bygninger på gården.
Ifølge politiet er det ikke kjent hva som er årsaken til brannen, og de vil etterforske saken videre.</description>

      <description>Ståle Solbakken har valgt ut følgende ellever til kampen mot Wales på Ullevaal:

CHEK https://cheknews.ca/ Independent and employee owned - local news stories, weather, sports, events and more Thu, 19 Nov 2026 02:33:23 +0000 en-CA hourly 1 https://cheknews.ca/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/cropped-CHEK-Mark-512x512-1-200x200.png?crop=1 CHEK https://cheknews.ca/ 32 32 70014466 Ottawa is reviewing Cadet and Junior Canadian programs, including those on Vancouver Island https://cheknews.ca/ottawa-is-reviewing-cadet-and-junior-canadian-programs-including-those-on-vancouver-island-1362465/ Thu, 19 Nov 2026 01:16:06 +0000 https://cheknews.ca/?p=1362465

Cadets and Junior Canadian Ranger programs are being paused in various parts of the country due to budgetary constraints.

]]>

Cadets and Junior Canadian Ranger programs are being paused in various parts of the country due to budgetary constraints.

In Nanaimo, navy cadets meet weekly to hone their life skills at the Navy League Training Centre on 5th Street.

On Tuesday, parents and trainees, received concerning emails. One email provided to CHEK News says that due to budgetary constraints the Cadets and Junior Canadian Rangers Group Pacific Region will implement temporary reductions to cadet activities for the remainder of the fiscal year ending March 31.

It said activities such as band, guard and marksmanship are paused. One Nanaimo parent says those are the activities that actually draw kids to the programs.

Michael Gendron, former cadet parent and program advocate back east, says he’s seen the value of the cadet program first-hand.

“We’re talking real life skills that were being taught to young Canadians through this program and it’s disappointing to see that the priorities have sort of shifted and the government which often says we support the aims of the program but they’re not putting their money where their mouths are,” said Gendron.

The Department of National Defense (DND) says the Cadets and Junior Canadian Rangers Group is reviewing its financial plan for the current fiscal year.

It notes the program received an additional $27 million in 2026, bringing its overall budget to approximately $265 million and says it’s focusing on reducing costs that do not directly support core activities and program delivery.

“Just from the sheer basic we know that the cost of everything is going up so in real dollars that might represent less spending authority even through the real dollar amount is larger,” said Gendron.

Watch the story in the video below:

Loading the player...

During his kids’ time in cadets Gendron says he saw opportunities becoming more limited for those enrolled. For example the amount of graduates who were able to take part in summer camps dropped.

Nanaimo-Ladysmith’s MP Tamara Kronis says the leadership programs have proven phenomenal for young Canadians.

“If there isn’t enough money for this, what on earth is this government spending its money on?” asked Kronis.

Kronis says people have been outraged by news of the temporary reductions saying she and her colleagues have been contacted non-stop about the issue since Monday.

“I think it’s imperative that the government now explain why they are making cuts instead of delivery on that promise to expand the programs,” said Kronis.

All the pressure may be having an impact. In a letter to parents and cadets Wednesday afternoon a Lieutenant with Nanaimo’s Sea Cadets program says she had a ‘positive update’ that while some activities may need to be adjusted or scaled back, optional training activities in Nanaimo, including band, guard and marksmanship will continue.

She warns though some “adjustments” may be necessary “as further direction is received.”

]]> 1362465 More seniors are staying in the workforce longer: report https://cheknews.ca/more-seniors-are-staying-in-the-workforce-longer-report-1362458/ Thu, 19 Nov 2026 01:02:01 +0000 https://cheknews.ca/?p=1362458

A multi-year report from the National Institute of Ageing has found that seniors are continuing to work longer, pushing the average retirement age to a new high in 50 years.

The post More seniors are staying in the workforce longer: report appeared first on CHEK.

]]>

A multi-year report from the National Institute of Ageing has found that seniors are continuing to work longer, pushing the average retirement age to a new high in 50 years.

Canada has received a “super-aged nation” status, according to a new report published by the National Institute of Ageing — meaning one in five people are over the age of 65.

“I’m not surprised,” said University of Victoria psychology professor Stuart MacDonald.

“I think in a lot of the conversations that I have, people [say] anecdotally that older adults are working longer, and I think there’s lots of reasons for that.”

The number of older people in the workforce has more than doubled since 2000, more than doubling from six per cent to 15.2 per cent — roughly 1.2 million people — in 2025.

That’s pushed the average retirement to its highest in 50 years, which is now 64.5 years, compared to 64.6 years in 1976. The lowest recorded retirement age was 60.9 years in 1997.

“Rising cost of living, particularly in context [sic] like Vancouver and Victoria,” said MacDonald.

Watch the story in the video below:

Loading the player...

The decision for workers to retire, according to the report, heavily differs, depending on their current financial stability.

The report said 64 per cent of workers who feel they make enough money could choose when they wanted to retire. In contrast, none of those surveyed who said they don’t feel like they make enough money are able to choose when to retire.

Forty-three per cent of workers between 65 to 74 say they are working out of necessity, compared to 57 per cent who say it’s a choice.

Former chef Terry Small says his decision to retire was a mix of necessity and choice. He stopped working in 2023 and admits the pandemic had an impact on his journey to retire.

He says he’s financially stable and won’t need to work again, but he’s worried for other seniors.

“I hope that people are able to manage and come along and find their way. It’s difficult with housing and the cost of living,” said Small.

For older people already in the workforce, they say it’s difficult to hold on to that job, citing discrimination, ageism, and lack of upskilling. In the last year, 70 per cent of respondents said they faced some form of discrimination, including being told jokes about their age and that they have difficulty understanding technology like computers.

Workplace training drops as workers get older. Only 31 per cent of respondents between the ages of 50 and 64 say they took part in workplace training. For those 65 to 79, that number dropped to 15 per cent.

“How do we ensure that there’s equitable access to lifelong training to keep up with things like artificial intelligence as it becomes more predominant in the workforce?” said Talia Bronstein, director of policy at the National Institute of Ageing.

With 20 per cent of the workforce made up of older people, the report is calling on all levels of government to take action, including creating age-inclusive workplaces, reducing financial barriers, and expanding training in the workplace.

A historic and powerful new company is being formed in Nanaimo as one of the area’s largest industrial employers joins forces with the Snuneymuxw First Nation, that has sprawling land up for development in its territory. 

“Today, Snuneymuxw and Harmac are deciding that we are better off building the future together,” said Snuneymuxw Elected Chief Mike Wyse (Xumtilum).

“From this point in time, we’re sharing our business together. But its really the future is where we are really going to be growing,” said Harmac-Pacific CEO and Paul Sadler.

Tuesday’s signing comes months after heated community opposition to Harmac-Pacific application to the City of Nanaimo to rezone 72 hectares of land that it owns near Cable Bay Trail, into heavy industrial lands. In April, Snuneymuxw wrote a letter stating that lands in that area are an integral part of its village site. At that time the Nation did not give its consent to rezoning, because consultation wasn’t complete.

“That’s a very significant piece of land that we have a lot of history. So the recognition is getting us to where we are today, and we’re going to sit down and talk and work together on future development and how that will look,” said Chief Wyse.

Watch the story in the video below:

Loading the player...

“The future for Snuneymuxw and for this community looks so much brighter than it was before that agreement was signed,” said Nanaimo Mayor Leonard Krog.

Snuneymuxw already owns a deep portfolio of companies, from fisheries and forestry, to real estate, including a Courtyard Marriott Hotel in Nanaimo, five casinos, a cannabis retail store, and a fashion line. SFN currently employs 1,800 people at its multiple branches.

What new developments this new company hopes to build, so far isn’t being disclosed. Yet those gathered for the announcement Tuesday applauded the goal behind it.

“To work together. It is a new chapter that has been unfolding on these lands for a very long time,” said Snuneymuxw Coun. Bill Yoachim.

“And lasting reconciliation it creates, for generations to come,” said Nanaimo-Lantzville MLA George Anderson.

Through a partnership, that both parties hope will carve out a new model for doing business in B.C.

]]> 1362210 ‘Buyers market’ and lower home prices not a cause for concern, say experts https://cheknews.ca/buyers-market-and-lower-home-prices-not-a-cause-for-concern-say-experts-1362402/ Thu, 19 Nov 2026 00:35:13 +0000 https://cheknews.ca/?p=1362402

A B.C. real estate search and data platform says half of the properties for sale in the capital city right now are listed below their assessed value.

The post ‘Buyers market’ and lower home prices not a cause for concern, say experts appeared first on CHEK.

]]>

A B.C. real estate search and data platform says half of the properties for sale in the capital city right now are listed below their assessed value.

Zealty.ca is reporting that as of Wednesday, 226 of 451 listings in Victoria are priced below their latest assessment.

CHEK News asked the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) if there is reason to be concerned.

“No,” said lead CMHC’s lead B.C. economist Shiva Moshtari Doust. “We should consider that assessments are reflective of what’s happened up to last year…That’s not reflective of today’s market.”

Generally speaking, as of November 2026, B.C.’s housing market is slow, soft, and largely buyer friendly.

“It is the best time to buy. If you are a buyer right now in this market it can’t be better than this,” said Hamidreza Etebarian, president of zealty.ca.

“Conditions have shifted more to a buyers market,” said Doust. “Still in the balanced territory, but buyers have more negotiation power.”

Watch the story in the video below:

Loading the player...

Slower sales are placing downward pressure on prices in most major markets, as inventory remains elevated relative to demand.

“As a result, the provincial average price was down 2.8 per cent year-over-year at about $950,000,” said BC Real Estate Association (BCREA) Chief Economist Brendon Ogmundson in a November report.

Vancouver Island Real Estate Board CEO Jason Yochim says on Vancouver Island, prices are being hit harder, but it’s worse on the mainland.

“From what I’ve heard of the mainland markets, there’s anywhere from 20 to 30 per cent decline. We’re not seeing that. Ours are more like 10 per cent,” said Yochim.

Those price adjustments, Doust says, are reflective of current supply and demand, the resale and job market, new home market, and a softer rental market.

That said, mortgage delinquency, has increased in B.C., according to data from a TransUnion report published on Aug. 25.

B.C. is among the top three provinces showing signs of financial strain, seeing a four-point increase between 2025 and 2026.

PEI saw an increase of five basis points, and Ontario six basis points.

Data from Zealty.ca is showing the highest number of court-ordered home listings in the Lower Mainland in a decade. 

“Our data is limited to Interior B.C., Greater Vancouver and the Fraser Valley, and if I speak to those, we’re seeing record, all time high of foreclosures listings in the past 10 years,” said Etebarian.

Nationally however, the increase on mortgage delinquency remains modest, according to TransUnion researchers. But those in more expensive housing markets with larger mortgage balances may “face greater exposure to affordability pressures and payment shocks,” the report reads.

Experts say, among Vancouver Island’s unique buyer demographic, those who are insulated by the Salish Sea, who already have equity, and are looking to retire or size up from the mainland, may absorb impacts more easily here.

“Where we anticipated that we may have had the biggest hurt were those mortgages that are coming up for renewal that were five-year mortgages, because they have to refinance at a higher rate than they did five years ago,” said Yochim. “But the impact wasn’t as great as we thought, and we’re not seeing those types of foreclosures and things we anticipated.”

With files from CBC.

Maj. Peter Headley has been charged with four military service offences related to his time as commander of Air Task Force Prestwick in the United Kingdom.

A statement from the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal says Headley has been charged with two counts of negligent performance of military duty, one count of abuse of subordinates and one count of conduct to the prejudice of good order and discipline.

The negligence and prejudice charges could result in dismissal with disgrace, while an abuse charge can result in a short prison term.

The provost marshal’s statement says the investigation was launched in July and Headley has returned to Canada and remains employed by the Royal Canadian Air Force.

If the charges result in prosecution, they will be heard by the military justice system, says the statement.

As with non-military criminal matters, the accused is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

Beach walkers at Goose Spit are being reminded of potential delays or detours while the Department of National Defence scours the historical defence lands for hazardous material, including unexploded ordnance.

The post National Defence uncovers exploded munition scraps at project site near Goose Spit, B.C. appeared first on CHEK.

]]>

Beach walkers at the popular Goose Spit coastal park are being reminded of potential delays or detours while the Department of National Defence is scanning and excavating the historical defence lands for hazardous material, including unexploded ordnance (UXO) that date back to the Second World War.

The DND’s surface and sub-surface scanning project of the defence lands near Goose Spit, south of Comox, started on Nov. 1 and is expected to continue through Dec. 15.

Maj. Ward Trythall, regional civil planner for the military and the project manager of the UXO Goose Spit scanning project, says a third-party consultant called Munitions Response Services (MRS) is handling the fieldwork with a crew of six to a dozen members.

“They’re, the experts in unexploded ordnance scanning and have done significant works across the country. And within B.C., certainly they’re still working on the UXO removal project in Vernon at what’s known as the Vernon Commons, and have been doing so for many years,” said Trythall.

On Nov. 13, Trythall, said the team had completed phase one of scanning and were starting phase two, where crews begin to excavate and retrieve their findings.

Findings reported so far

After completing the first phase of scanning, crews found pieces of unexploded ordnance, but none intact to date. 

“To date, we have not found any UXO, defined as actually intact, unexploded ordnance,” he said, adding, “We have found some, what we call munition scrap, which is pieces of ordnance that are on the land. For the most part, that’s been old, small arms ammunition, expended small arms ammunition. Typically they’ve been what we call blank rounds, so they were used for training, and a couple of pieces of exploded munition of some sort.”

According to Trythall, the area on Goose Spit was an active Canadian military training site in World War II. However, there are gaps in the land records in terms of risk assessments, so this project is the DND’s commitment to due diligence and risk assessment activities required on the defence lands.

He says they’ve uncovered mainly fragments, adding that the bulk of their findings are old steel rods and pieces of fence posts.

Safety near potential explosives

Now in phase two, crews are starting to dig out their findings. 

Trythall explains it’s “where we are actually going along and excavating each of the targets, we’re only approximately five, 10 per cent in so far and that’s the extent of what we found.”

Crews are excavating these decades-old items by hand.

“So far, our expectation is that most of the munition scrap dates from the Second World War. We started the project, having done a thorough record search of modern Canadian Armed Forces records, and we’re able to satisfy ourselves that in modern times, records dating back in theory, similar to the early 1970s, that there was no expectation that there would be dangerous, unexploded ordnance on the spit, because the area had not been approved for use of those types of ammunition on the spit in that period up to today.”

However, they treat each retrieval as a potential risk and that’s why the public is being asked to keep a 60 metre distance from the exclusion zone.

“Every target represents a risk until we’ve identified it satisfactorily. So what we’re establishing around the target, any given excavation is that 60 metre exclusion zone. So within that zone, the operators are the only ones inside that for safety purposes, the archeological team moves back,” he says.

The exclusion zone is marked with signage and crews are on site to provide direction near the area.

He asks the public to be mindful when crews are working at the edge of the defence lands property where it overlaps with the public beach.

“And because the DND lands extend right to what’s known as the natural boundary, or the high tide mark, if we are excavating a target that’s right at the edge of the land boundary with the intertidal zone…That 60-metre exclusion zone can impact travel along the beach and that is really our biggest safety concern for us,” he says.

“When members of the public encounter those signs, our simple ask is, please respect them and understand that those exclusion zones are for their safety, just in case we do happen upon something that is dangerous, so that an accident, if it ever occurred while they’re excavating, has a very limited impact upon anybody who may be outside that 60-metre zone.”

First Nation land

Tryhall adds that project was initiated due to the Goose Spit lands being divested by B.C. to the Ko’mox First Nation’s treaty settlement lands.

“Because DND was occupying those lands under an Order in Council, granted by the provincial government 70 years ago, the arrangement and agreement within the treaty is that certain lands will be divested to the K’ómoks Nation and the K’ómoks Nation will grant a subsequent tenure to National Defence for our continued use, where we have uses on the Goose Spit Peninsula right now.”

K’ómoks First Nation (KFN) explains how the Goose Spit is broken up into four different parcels: “The first is the stretch of road, which is governed by Area B of the CVRD. The second is the HMCS Quadra Cadet Base. The third piece is our Indian Reserve #3, and the fourth is what we have been calling the ‘tip’ of the spit, which was offered and accepted by KFN as part of the Agreement in Principle.”

“There is currently no lease with DND for the use of our reserve lands,” says the KFN.

The nation is currently negotiating a lease agreement with the DND to use the “tip” of the Spit for specific purposes when needed.

“The HMCS Quadra Cadet Base is legally owned by B.C. and is being used by DND under an Order in Council with Canada. The Treaty, if approved, will include the transfer of the full Goose Spit to the KFN, including HMCS Quadra, which includes the cadet camp,” adds the KFN.
